title: Three strands, four workers
hookLine: Krishna sorts workers the way a foreman might, by what drives them, and then adds a worker the strands can't hold
carry: the gunas sort the worker, not the job

lines: WHAT KIND OF WORKER ARE YOU?
cards: What kind of worker are you? Not how fast, not how skilled. What's going on inside while the work gets done.

Krishna is near the end of his time on earth, and his friend Uddhava is getting his last teachings, so Krishna packs in what matters. He sorts workers the way a careful foreman might, by what drives them.
He reaches for the three gunas, the strands from the Samkhya weeks, sattva, rajas and tamas: clear, restless, heavy. Every kind of work can be read through them, he says, and so can every worker.
Then, at the end of the list, he names one more worker, a kind the strands can't hold.

teach.b: Here's the sorting, in paraphrase. A worker free of attachment is in sattva. A worker blinded by wanting things for himself is in rajas.
A worker who has lost the sense of what to do and what not to do is in tamas. And a worker who has taken refuge in him, Krishna says, is beyond the strands altogether. He reads the work the same way.

teach.h: WORK OFFERED, WORK FOR GAIN, WORK TO HARM.
teach.b: Work offered to him, done without hunger for its fruit, is sattvic. Work done for what it will bring is rajasic. Work done to harm is tamasic.
This is the Hindu teaching of the gunas, and families still use it every day, for food, for sleep, for habits, as well as for work. Notice what isn't on the list: any particular job.

teach.h: THE GUNAS SORT THE WORKER, NOT THE JOB.
teach.b: The gunas don't sort cleaners from surgeons. They sort the inside.
Two people can carry the same boxes up the same stairs for a friend who's moving, one for praise and one as an offering, and in these verses they're doing different karma.
On the path of action, the task is the same size for everyone. What changes is the hand behind it.

teach.h: A FOURTH WORKER: BEYOND THE STRANDS.
teach.b: And the fourth worker? Krishna doesn't describe a better technique. He describes a relationship: refuge in God.
For devotees of Krishna, that's where the path of action is headed.

how: Hindu teachers use the three gunas to talk about the quality of everyday work and food and habits, and in the Bhagavata's eleventh book Krishna applies them to the worker and the work, with a fourth kind beyond the gunas for one who takes refuge in him.

o: a ranking of jobs from noble to lowly
a wage paid out for each finished job
work, read by what drives the one doing it

p: lost the sense of what to do

s: in the Uddhava Gita, some jobs are sattvic and others are tamasic
the strands sort what's driving the worker, not the job.
Krishna describes a worker beyond all three strands
the one who has taken refuge in him.
work done without hunger for its fruit is called rajasic
that's sattvic. rajasic work is done for the sake of what it will bring.

games.q: two people carry the same boxes for a friend who's moving. one does it for praise; one does it as an offering, wanting nothing back. in the Uddhava Gita's terms, what's different?
o: only how fast the boxes get moved.
games.why: Krishna sorts work by what drives it: done for gain it's rajasic, offered without hunger for fruit it's sattvic. same boxes, different work.

practice: Picture starting the next task waiting for you, a phone call, an email, a drive, and notice what's already there inside: an eagerness for a result, a heaviness, a calm, with no grading.
Then picture starting it once more, and see whether simply noticing what drives you changes anything. If you pray, you can offer that task to the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Work, sorted in the Uddhava Gita by the worker's inside: unattached, driven, fogged, or beyond the strands altogether.

orig.note: Sanskrit: beyond the gunas, the three strands; Krishna's word for the worker who has taken refuge in him.

carryVoice: Your line: the gunas sort the worker, not the job. Same boxes, same stairs; the difference is the hand. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.25.23 (work offered to him without desire for fruit is sattvic; for results, rajasic; given to violence, tamasic)
Bhagavata Purana 11.25.26 (the worker free of attachment, blinded by desire, devoid of judgment; and the one who has taken refuge in him, beyond the gunas)
Samkhya Karika 12–13 (the three gunas, recalled from days 1172–1173)
